V3-001.topic: CSF lactate on the blood-gas analyser: cut-off and why it rises
V3-001.q: Fever and altered sensorium: what will you do with the CSF in the ABG machine, what cut-off do you use, and why is CSF lactate high in bacterial meningitis?
a: What I do: after the LP, run a fresh CSF sample on the ICU **blood-gas analyser**. Lactate (and glucose) in 2 minutes, long before the cell count and Gram stain. Blood-gas analysers read CSF lactate reliably (r = **0.94** against the laboratory; Stephani 2021).
Cut-off: **>3.5 mmol/L** (about 32 mg/dL) favours bacterial. Meta-analysis optimum: **35 mg/dL = 3.9 mmol/L** (Sakushima 2011). To convert: mg/dL ÷ 9 = mmol/L.
Accuracy (Sakushima 2011, 33 studies): sensitivity **0.93**, specificity **0.96**. Huy 2010 (25 studies): AUC 0.98, better than cells, glucose or protein alone.

Why it rises: CSF lactate is made inside the CNS and is independent of blood lactate. Brain made ischaemic by low flow, vasculitis and raised ICP switches to **anaerobic glycolysis**; neutrophils and bacteria in the CSF add their own lactate.
Glucose on the same run: pair it with a simultaneous blood glucose. CSF:blood ratio **<0.4** supports bacterial.

Caution: after antibiotics sensitivity falls to **0.49**, so a normal value does not exclude bacterial meningitis. Falsely high with a bloody tap or delayed processing; also raised after neurosurgery, seizures, haemorrhage or stroke.
V3-001.src: Sakushima K et al., J Infect 2011;62:255; Huy NT et al., Crit Care 2010;14:R240; Stephani C, Choi AHK, Moerer O, Intensive Care Med Exp 2021;9

V3-002.topic: CT before LP: who needs it, the evidence, and the CT findings
V3-002.q: Who needs a CT before lumbar puncture in suspected meningitis, can you do LP without CT, and what does CT show?
a: Rule: most patients need **no CT**. If CT is needed, take blood cultures and give dexamethasone and antibiotics **first**, then scan, then LP (IDSA 2004).

Criteria | UK 2016 | ESCMID 2016 | IDSA 2004
Consciousness | **GCS ≤12** | **GCS <10** | any abnormal
Focal deficit | yes | yes | yes
Seizures | continuous / uncontrolled | new onset | new, within 1 week
Other triggers: papilloedema (UK, IDSA); severe immunocompromise (ESCMID, IDSA); history of CNS disease such as mass, stroke or focal infection (IDSA only).

Evidence: Glimåker 2018, 815 Swedish adults. IDSA criteria would scan **65%**, ESCMID **32%**, Swedish **7%**. Prompt LP vs CT first: lower mortality (adjusted OR **0.38**), more favourable outcome (OR **2.11**).
So LP without CT is right when no criterion is present. A normal CT does not remove the risk if there are clinical signs of impending herniation.

CT findings: often normal early. Look for cerebral oedema, effacement of basal cisterns, **hydrocephalus**, **infarcts** (vasculitis, venous thrombosis), cerebritis or abscess, subdural empyema, and meningeal enhancement with contrast.
Also the source: sinusitis, mastoiditis, skull base fracture or pneumocephalus. MRI with gadolinium is better for enhancement, ventriculitis and early infarcts.
V3-002.src: Tunkel AR et al., IDSA, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267; van de Beek D et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22:S37; McGill F et al., UK joint specialist societies, J Infect 2016;72:405; Glimåker M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2018;66:321

V3-003.topic: Empirical treatment of community-acquired bacterial meningitis
V3-003.q: How do you treat community-acquired bacterial meningitis empirically, and when do you add ampicillin?
a: First: blood cultures, then **dexamethasone 10 mg IV** just before or with the first antibiotic. Do not wait for CT or LP.
Base: **ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly** (or cefotaxime 2 g 4–6-hourly).
Plus **vancomycin** (15–20 mg/kg 8–12-hourly) where cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus is possible; rifampicin is the alternative.
Add **ampicillin 2 g IV 4-hourly** for Listeria if: age **>50** (ESCMID, IDSA; UK 2016 uses **≥60**), pregnancy, immunosuppression or transplant, malignancy, diabetes, alcoholism or cirrhosis.
Why ampicillin: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins, so ceftriaxone alone never covers it. Listeria peaks at the age extremes.
If encephalitis is possible (seizures, focal signs, behaviour change): add **aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly** until HSV PCR returns.
Then narrow to the organism and Gram stain. Duration: meningococcus 7 days, pneumococcus 10–14, Listeria at least 21.
V3-003.src: Tunkel AR et al., IDSA, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267; van de Beek D et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22:S37; Farkas J, IBCC: Approach to CNS infection (EMCrit)

V3-004.topic: Dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis: de Gans 2002 and the window
V3-004.q: Dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis: what did de Gans 2002 show, can you start it once antibiotics have gone in, and when do you stop it?
a: de Gans 2002 (NEJM): **301** adults, dexamethasone **10 mg** 15–20 min before or with the first antibiotic, then 6-hourly for **4 days**.
Result: unfavourable outcome **15% vs 25%** (RR 0.59), death **7% vs 15%** (RR 0.48).
Pneumococcal subgroup: unfavourable outcome **26% vs 52%**, death **14% vs 34%**. The benefit is mainly pneumococcal.
Why timing matters: antibiotics lyse bacteria and release cell-wall products that drive the cytokine surge. Dexamethasone must be on board before or with that lysis.
Already given antibiotics? **ESCMID 2016**: still start up to **4 h** after the first dose, not later. **IDSA 2004**: do not start. UK 2016: may consider up to 12 h.

Continue or stop: IDSA continues only if Gram-positive diplococci or **S. pneumoniae** grow. ESCMID continues for **pneumococcal or H. influenzae** and advises considering stopping for other organisms; stop for **Listeria** (higher mortality with dexamethasone) or if not bacterial.
Not routine in HSV encephalitis.
V3-004.src: de Gans J, van de Beek D, NEJM 2002;347:1549; van de Beek D et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22:S37; Tunkel AR et al., IDSA, Clin Infect Dis 2004;39:1267

V3-005.topic: Steroids in TB meningitis: Thwaites 2004 and ACT HIV 2023
V3-005.q: What is the role of steroids in tuberculous meningitis, and what did the ACT HIV trial show?
a: Why: thick basal exudate causes hydrocephalus, vasculitic infarcts and cranial nerve palsies. Steroids damp that inflammation.
Thwaites 2004 (NEJM): **545** patients over 14 years in Vietnam, dexamethasone vs placebo, tapered over 6–8 weeks by severity grade.
Result: death at 9 months **31.8% vs 41.3%**, RR **0.69** (95% CI 0.52–0.92), p = 0.01. No fewer severely disabled survivors (18.2% vs 13.8%). Fewer serious adverse events.
HIV subgroup in Thwaites: only **98** patients, no significant effect. Too small to answer, hence ACT HIV.

ACT HIV (Donovan, NEJM 2023): **520** HIV-positive adults, Vietnam and Indonesia, 6–8-week taper. Death at 12 months **44.1% vs 49.0%**, HR **0.85** (0.66–1.10), p = 0.22. No benefit on any secondary end point.

WHO (2022, maintained 2025): dexamethasone or prednisolone tapered over **6–8 weeks** in all TB meningitis, strong recommendation. Adult dose about **0.4 mg/kg/day**, then taper. India (ICMR STW 2022): **8–12 weeks** in total.
So: give it to every HIV-negative patient. In HIV the survival benefit is unproven: weigh it case by case (raised ICP, IRIS).
V3-005.src: Thwaites GE et al., NEJM 2004;351:1741; Donovan J et al., NEJM 2023;389:1357 (ACT HIV); WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 4: treatment and care, 2025 (recommendation maintained); ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow, NTEP TB meningitis, 2022

V3-006.topic: Viral meningitis and HSV encephalitis: start aciclovir empirically
V3-006.q: How do you treat viral meningitis and suspected HSV encephalitis, and for how long do you give aciclovir?
a: Viral meningitis: usually **enterovirus**, self-limiting. Supportive care: analgesia, antipyretics, fluids.
Encephalitis means the brain is involved: altered sensorium, behaviour change, seizures, focal signs. Then treat as HSV.
Start **IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly** in every patient with suspected encephalitis, at once, pending HSV PCR and MRI (IDSA 2008, A-III). Do not wait for results.
Why urgent: treated HSV encephalitis still had **28%** mortality at 18 months, falling to **8%** when aciclovir started within 4 days of onset.
Duration: **14–21 days** (IDSA); 14 if immunocompetent, 21 if immunocompromised (UK). Neonates: 20 mg/kg 8-hourly for 21 days.
Early PCR can be falsely negative. If it is negative but the picture or MRI fits, keep aciclovir and repeat the PCR in **3–7 days**.
Caution: crystal nephropathy. Adjust the dose to renal function and keep the patient well hydrated.
V3-006.src: Tunkel AR et al., IDSA encephalitis guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2008;47:303; Solomon T et al., UK national guideline (ABN/BIA), J Infect 2012;64:347

V3-007.topic: FOUR score vs GCS in the ICU
V3-007.q: What is the FOUR score, how is it scored, and why is it better than GCS for intubated patients?
a: **FOUR score** (Full Outline of UnResponsiveness; **Wijdicks, Ann Neurol 2005**): four parts, each **0–4**, total **0–16**. Validated in **120 ICU patients**; inter-rater agreement as good as GCS (weighted κ **0.82**).
**E** eye: 4 open and tracking, or blinking to command | 3 open, not tracking | 2 opens to loud voice | 1 opens to pain | 0 stays closed to pain.
**M** motor: 4 thumbs-up, fist or peace sign to command | 3 localises pain | 2 flexion | 1 extension | 0 none, or generalised myoclonus status.
**B** brainstem: 4 pupil and corneal reflexes present | 3 one pupil wide and fixed | 2 pupil or corneal absent | 1 both absent | 0 pupil, corneal and cough all absent.
**R** respiration: 4 not intubated, regular | 3 not intubated, Cheyne–Stokes | 2 not intubated, irregular | 1 breathes above the ventilator rate | 0 breathes at the ventilator rate, or apnoea.

Why it suits the ICU: **no verbal component**, so an intubated patient gets a full score (GCS can only record VT). Eye tracking and blinking detect **locked-in syndrome**; pupils and breathing pattern track **herniation**.
It separates patients who all score GCS 3, and the lowest FOUR totals carried a higher in-hospital mortality than the lowest GCS totals.
Catch: GCS is still the language of TBI guidelines, triage and trials (BTF severity bands). Best answer: record both; follow the intubated or comatose patient with FOUR.
V3-007.src: Wijdicks EFM et al., Ann Neurol 2005;58:585-593 (FOUR score validation)

V3-008.q: What is cerebral autoregulation, and how do you individualise the CPP target with PRx and CPPopt?
a: Autoregulation: cerebral arterioles constrict as pressure rises and dilate as it falls, keeping CBF steady over a plateau (classically **MAP 50–150 mmHg**, Lassen). Below it: ischaemia. Above it: hyperaemia and oedema.
In the injured brain the plateau narrows, shifts right or is lost. CBF becomes pressure-passive, so one fixed CPP can be too low for one patient and too high for another.

**PRx** (pressure reactivity index; **Czosnyka, Neurosurgery 1997**): a moving Pearson correlation between slow waves of MAP and ICP. Near zero or negative = vessels react (intact). Positive = pressure-passive (impaired).

Thresholds (**Sorrentino, Neurocrit Care 2012**; 459 TBI patients): PRx above **0.25** linked to death, above **0.05** to unfavourable outcome. In practice, a sustained PRx above about **0.2–0.3** = impaired autoregulation.

**CPPopt** (**Steiner, Crit Care Med 2002**): plot PRx against CPP; the lowest point of the U-shaped curve is the CPP where autoregulation works best. Aries (Crit Care Med 2012) automated it on a moving **4 h** window.
**COGiTATE** (Tas, J Neurotrauma 2021): 60 TBI patients, 4 centres. Targeting CPPopt was **feasible and safe** (in target **46.5%** of the time). Outcome benefit is not yet tested.

What I do: BTF CPP **60–70 mmHg**; with PRx, aim near CPPopt. Without PRx, the SIBICC Tier 2 MAP challenge: raise MAP and watch ICP. ICP falls or stays flat = autoregulation intact; ICP rises = impaired.
V3-008.src: Czosnyka M et al., Neurosurgery 1997;41:11; Steiner LA et al., Crit Care Med 2002;30:733; Aries MJH et al., Crit Care Med 2012;40:2456; Sorrentino E et al., Neurocrit Care 2012;16:258; Tas J et al., J Neurotrauma 2021;38:2790 (COGiTATE); Carney N et al., Neurosurgery 2017;80:6 (BTF 4th ed.); Hawryluk GWJ et al., Intensive Care Med 2019;45:1783 (SIBICC)

V3-009.topic: Acute SCI: 2024 MAP targets, early surgery, steroid positions
V3-009.q: What MAP do you target in acute spinal cord injury today, and where do steroids stand after NASCIS?
a: MAP (**Kwon, Global Spine J 2024**; AO Spine/Praxis update of the 2013 AANS/CNS guideline): augment MAP to a floor of **75–80 mmHg**, do not actively push beyond **90–95**, for about **3–7 days**. Weak recommendation, very low-quality evidence.

Why: the injured cord loses autoregulation and neurogenic shock is common, so hypoperfusion adds secondary ischaemia. No recommendation on vasopressor choice or spinal cord perfusion pressure targets.

The old **MAP 85–90 for 7 days** was the 2013 Level III target. **Sajdeya, JAMA Netw Open 2025** (92 patients; MAP >85–90 vs >65–70): no neurological gain; more respiratory complications (**78% vs 39%**) and longer ventilation.
Surgery: early decompression **within 24 h** of injury is recommended for adults at any level (**Fehlings, Global Spine J 2024**; strong, moderate-quality evidence).

NASCIS II (Bracken, NEJM 1990): methylprednisolone **30 mg/kg** bolus, then **5.4 mg/kg/h for 23 h**. Primary outcome negative; benefit only in a post hoc subgroup treated within 8 h. NASCIS III (JAMA 1997): 48 h for 3–8 h starts (subgroup); more severe pneumonia (**5.8% vs 2.6%**).

Positions: AANS/CNS 2013: methylprednisolone **not recommended** (Level I). AO Spine 2017 (Fehlings): suggest offering a **24-h infusion if started within 8 h**; not after 8 h; not a 48-h course (all weak).
Other targets: avoid hypotension and hypoxia; VTE prophylaxis **within 72 h**; no hypotonic fluids; watch breathing and bradycardia in cervical injury.
V3-009.src: Kwon BK et al., Global Spine J 2024;14(3 Suppl):187S-211S (haemodynamic management); Fehlings MG et al., Global Spine J 2024;14(3 Suppl):174S-186S (timing of decompression); Sajdeya R et al., JAMA Netw Open 2025;8(9):e2525364; Bracken MB et al., NEJM 1990;322:1405 (NASCIS II); Bracken MB et al., JAMA 1997;277:1597 (NASCIS III); Hurlbert RJ et al., Neurosurgery 2013;72 Suppl 2:93 (AANS/CNS); Fehlings MG et al., Global Spine J 2017;7(3 Suppl):203S-211S (methylprednisolone)

V3-010.topic: Brain stem death in India: Form 10 and the 2026 national guideline
V3-010.q: How do you certify brain stem death in India under the THOA rules and the 2026 national guideline?
a: Law: **THOA 1994** (amended 2011; Rules **2014**) recognises brain stem death. Certified on **Form 10** by a board of four: hospital medical administrator, an authorised specialist, a neurologist or neurosurgeon, and the treating doctor.

No neurologist or neurosurgeon: a surgeon or physician plus an anaesthetist or intensivist, nominated by the administrator. Two examinations at least **6 h apart** in adults; longer in children, at the board's discretion.

**National Guidelines on Brain Stem Death Certification, Edition I, 2026** (MoHFW/NOTTO), prerequisites: core temp **≥36 °C**; SBP **≥100** or MAP **≥60**; SpO₂ ≥94%; pH 7.20–7.50; Na **125–159**; sedatives cleared (**5 half-lives**).
Apnoea test: 100% O₂ for **10 min**; disconnect; O₂ catheter near the carina at **4–6 L/min**; watch chest and abdomen for **8–10 min**; ABG at about 8 min. PaCO₂ rises about 3 mmHg/min.

Positive: no breathing with PaCO₂ **≥60 mmHg and ≥20 above baseline**. Abort and reconnect if SBP **<90**, SpO₂ **<85% for >30 s** or instability; then an ancillary test (angiography, CT angiography, nuclear scan, TCD).
After targeted temperature management: wait for normothermia and at least **24 h** after rewarming. Record the time of death at the second positive determination; all members sign.

Live issue: on 28 Apr 2026 the Supreme Court (Dr S Ganapathy's petition) asked the **AIIMS** neurology head to form a 3–5 member committee on apnoea test safety and his proposed alternatives (angiography, EEG). Judgment reported reserved, Nov 2026.

Donation is separate: the 2026 guideline says certification is an independent medical and legal duty, never influenced by donation. If donation is declined, ventilation may be withdrawn per hospital and State procedure.
V3-010.src: Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Rules 2014, Form 10; National Guidelines on Brain Stem Death Certification, Edition I, MoHFW/NOTTO 2026; Greer DM et al., Neurology 2023;101:1112 (AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM brain death guideline); Supreme Court of India, Dr S Ganapathy v State of Kerala, order 28 Apr 2026 (LiveLaw); judgment reserved Nov 2026 (press reports)

V3-011.topic: Mannitol vs hypertonic saline: mechanism and evidence
V3-011.q: Mannitol or hypertonic saline for raised ICP: how does each work, and what does the evidence say?
a: **Both** raise plasma osmolality and draw water out of brain where the blood–brain barrier is intact. Both buy time; neither treats the cause.
**Mannitol** acts in two phases: first rheological (plasma expands, blood viscosity falls, autoregulating arterioles constrict, so cerebral blood volume falls within minutes), then osmotic.
Mannitol then causes an **osmotic diuresis**: hypovolaemia and hypotension follow unless urine is replaced. A poor fit for the bleeding, hypotensive trauma patient.
**Hypertonic saline** stays in the vessels and expands volume, so it suits low MAP. Costs: hypernatraemia, hyperchloraemic acidosis, volume overload, and a central line for 23.4%.
Evidence: both lower ICP; **no trial shows better functional outcome** with either. BTF 4th ed.: insufficient evidence to choose an agent. SIBICC 2019: no preference, same limits.
**NCS 2020**: suggests HTS over mannitol for initial ICP control in TBI (conditional, low quality); mannitol is an effective alternative; neither should be expected to improve outcome.
**COBI** (Roquilly, JAMA 2021; 370 pts): continuous 20% saline vs standard care in moderate–severe TBI. 6-month GOS-E adjusted OR **1.02** (0.71–1.47): no benefit. Use boluses, not infusions.
What I say: hypotensive or hypovolaemic → HTS; Na already near **155** or hyperchloraemic → mannitol. Bolus for an ICP rise; usual limits **Na 155, osmolality 320**, the same for both agents.
V3-011.src: Cook AM et al., NCS cerebral oedema guideline, Neurocrit Care 2020;32:647; Hawryluk GWJ et al., SIBICC, Intensive Care Med 2019;45:1783; Carney N et al., BTF 4th ed., Neurosurgery 2017;80:6; Roquilly A et al., JAMA 2021;325:2056 (COBI); Muizelaar JP et al., J Neurosurg 1983;59:822

V3-012.topic: Mannitol monitoring: osmolar gap, AKI and rebound
V3-012.q: How do you dose and monitor mannitol, and why use the osmolar gap rather than serum osmolality?
a: **Dose**: 0.25–1 g/kg IV bolus (20%) when ICP rises. Intermittent as needed, never a scheduled 4–6-hourly dose or a continuous infusion (SIBICC "do not" list).
Why not serum osmolality alone: it rises with sodium, glucose and urea too, so it cannot tell you how much **mannitol** is still circulating.
**Osmolar gap** = measured osmolality − calculated (2 × Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8, in mg/dL). Mannitol is an unmeasured osmole, so the gap tracks its blood level.
Practice: check the gap before each repeat dose. A trough gap under about **20 mOsm/kg** means mannitol has cleared and redosing is reasonable; a gap that stays high means it is accumulating.
**NCS 2020**: monitor mannitol by the **osmolar gap** rather than by an osmolality threshold; no cut-off has been validated in trials.
**AKI** is concentration-related: monitor creatinine and urine output, replace urine losses, avoid repeated doses in renal failure. NCS: an osmolality above 320 did not predict AKI.
**Rebound**: repeated doses let mannitol leak into injured brain where the barrier is broken; the gradient reverses and ICP rises again. One more reason for bolus-only dosing.
V3-012.src: Cook AM et al., NCS cerebral oedema guideline, Neurocrit Care 2020;32:647; Hawryluk GWJ et al., SIBICC, Intensive Care Med 2019;45:1783

V3-013.topic: Why DECRA was worse: design, imbalance and critique
V3-013.q: Why did early decompressive craniectomy in DECRA give worse outcomes?
a: **DECRA** (Cooper, NEJM 2011): 155 adults aged 15–59 with severe **diffuse** TBI, within 72 h; ICP **>20 mmHg for >15 min within 1 h** despite first-tier therapy.
Operation: **bifrontotemporoparietal** craniectomy; the sagittal sinus and **falx were not divided**. Randomised at a median of about 35 h after injury.
Result: ICP fell (mean 14.4 vs 19.1 mmHg), mortality the same (**19% vs 18%**), but unfavourable GOS-E **70% vs 51%** (OR 2.21).
Reason 1, **too early and too low a trigger**: 15 min above 20 mmHg is not truly refractory ICP; many controls would have settled with medical therapy.
Reason 2, **baseline imbalance**: both pupils unreactive in **27% vs 12%**. Adjusted post hoc for this, unfavourable outcome was no longer significant (OR **1.90**, 95% CI 0.95–3.79, p = 0.07).
Reason 3, **technique and harm**: bifrontal without falx division, with more surgical complications such as hydrocephalus. **15 of 82** controls (18%) also had lifesaving DC after 72 h.
Contrast **RESCUEicp**: DC as a last tier for ICP **>25 for 1–12 h** cut deaths but raised vegetative and dependent survival; at 12 months favourable outcome **45.4% vs 32.4%**.
V3-013.src: Cooper DJ et al., NEJM 2011;364:1493 (DECRA); Hutchinson PJ et al., NEJM 2016;375:1119 (RESCUEicp)

V3-014.topic: Hypothermia in TBI: why Eurotherm stopped, what POLAR showed
V3-014.q: What is the role of therapeutic hypothermia in TBI, and why was Eurotherm3235 stopped?
a: Rationale: cooling lowers cerebral metabolism, blood volume and ICP. The trials asked whether that improves outcome.
**Eurotherm3235** (Andrews, NEJM 2015): ICP **>20 mmHg for ≥5 min** despite stage-1 therapy, up to 10 days after injury; **32–35 °C** for ≥48 h plus standard care vs standard care.
Stopped early at **387** of 600 planned, on the independent monitoring committee's advice, because outcomes, including deaths, were **worse with cooling**. Not futility, not benefit.
Result: fewer stage-3 therapies were needed (44% vs 54%), yet unfavourable GOS-E **74.3% vs 63.5%**; adjusted OR **1.53** for a worse outcome; deaths by 6 months **34.9% vs 26.6%**.
Lesson: controlling the ICP number did not give a better brain; the systemic harms of cooling outweighed it.
**POLAR** (Cooper, JAMA 2018): 511 severe TBI, early prophylactic cooling to **33 °C**, started within 3 h of injury, for ≥72 h (up to 7 days) vs normothermia.
POLAR result: favourable GOS-E **48.8% vs 49.1%**, no benefit; more pneumonia (70.5% vs 57.1%, per protocol) and bradycardia (18.8% vs 4.2%).
Now: no prophylactic hypothermia (BTF IIB); SIBICC keeps **mild hypothermia 35–36 °C** as a Tier 3 option only. Always prevent fever.
V3-014.src: Andrews PJD et al., NEJM 2015;373:2403 (Eurotherm3235); Cooper DJ et al., JAMA 2018;320:2211 (POLAR); Hawryluk GWJ et al., SIBICC, Intensive Care Med 2019;45:1783; Carney N et al., BTF 4th ed., Neurosurgery 2017;80:6

V3-015.topic: Transfusion in acute brain injury: TRAIN, HEMOTION, SAHaRA
V3-015.q: What is the transfusion threshold in acute brain injury, and did liberal transfusion improve neurological outcome?
a: The general ICU trigger of **7 g/dL** comes from non-neurological trials. Injured brain with lost autoregulation may need more oxygen delivery, so three trials tested a higher trigger.
**TRAIN** (Taccone, JAMA 2024): 820 adults with TBI, SAH or ICH, GCS ≤13; transfuse at **<9 vs <7 g/dL**. Unfavourable GOS-E at 180 days **62.6% vs 72.6%** (RR 0.86): liberal better.
TRAIN also: less cerebral ischaemia (8.8% vs 13.5%); 28-day mortality similar (20.7% vs 22.5%).
**HEMOTION** (Turgeon, NEJM 2024): 742 moderate–severe TBI (GCS 3–12); **≤10 vs ≤7**. Unfavourable GOS-E at 6 months **68.4% vs 73.5%**; difference 5.4 points (95% CI −2.9 to 13.7): not significant.
**SAHaRA** (English, NEJM 2025): 742 aneurysmal SAH; **≤10 vs ≤8**. mRS ≥4 at 12 months **33.5% vs 37.7%** (RR 0.88, 0.72–1.09): not significant; less radiographic vasospasm with liberal.
Reading: all three lean towards liberal; only TRAIN reached significance. TRAIN and HEMOTION showed no major safety signal, but the liberal arms used far more blood.
What I do: in acute brain injury I do not wait for 7; I transfuse at about **9 g/dL**, with a lower bar if PbtO2 is low or vasospasm is active.
V3-015.src: Taccone FS et al., JAMA 2024;332:1623 (TRAIN); Turgeon AF et al., NEJM 2024;391:722 (HEMOTION); English SW et al., NEJM 2025;392:1079 (SAHaRA)

V3-016.topic: CT spotter: extradural vs subdural haematoma
V3-016.q: Spotter: CT head with an extra-axial collection. Extradural or subdural, and how do you tell?
a: **Extradural (EDH)**: between skull and dura. **Biconvex (lens-shaped)**, sharply defined, hyperdense; does **not cross sutures**, where the dura is fixed, but can cross the midline.
EDH cause: usually a temporal fracture tearing the **middle meningeal artery**, in younger patients. A **lucid interval** is classic but seen only in a minority.
**Subdural (SDH)**: between dura and arachnoid. **Crescent-shaped**, follows the hemisphere, **crosses sutures** but not the falx or tentorium.
SDH cause: torn **bridging veins** from acceleration–deceleration; elderly, atrophy, alcohol, anticoagulants. Underlying brain injury is common, so prognosis is worse than EDH.
SDH density with time: acute hyperdense; subacute (days to about 3 weeks) isodense and easy to miss; chronic hypodense. Mixed density or a swirl in an acute clot suggests active bleeding.
Report: side, thickness, **midline shift**, basal cisterns, contusions, and volume by **ABC/2**.
V3-016.src: Bullock MR et al., Surgical management of acute epidural hematomas, Neurosurgery 2006;58(3 Suppl):S7–S15; Bullock MR et al., Surgical management of acute subdural hematomas, Neurosurgery 2006;58(3 Suppl):S16–S24; standard neuroradiology teaching

V3-017.topic: Surgery for EDH and acute SDH: BTF criteria
V3-017.q: Which extradural and subdural haematomas need urgent surgery?
a: **EDH >30 cm³: evacuate**, whatever the GCS.
EDH can be observed with serial CT in a neurosurgical centre if **<30 cm³, <15 mm thick, <5 mm midline shift, GCS >8** and no focal deficit.
EDH in coma (**GCS <9**) with **anisocoria**: evacuate as soon as possible.
**Acute SDH >10 mm thick or midline shift >5 mm: evacuate**, whatever the GCS.
Smaller SDH in coma (GCS <9): operate if GCS falls by **≥2** from injury to admission, pupils are asymmetric or fixed and dilated, or ICP stays **>20 mmHg**.
Timing: as soon as possible once indicated. Craniotomy for EDH; craniotomy with or without bone-flap removal and duraplasty for SDH.
These criteria come from the BTF surgical guidelines (Bullock, Neurosurgery 2006); the BTF 4th ed. (2016) covers medical care and did not re-review them.
V3-017.src: Bullock MR et al., Surgical management of acute epidural hematomas, Neurosurgery 2006;58(3 Suppl):S7–S15; Bullock MR et al., Surgical management of acute subdural hematomas, Neurosurgery 2006;58(3 Suppl):S16–S24

V3-018.topic: Status epilepticus: ILAE time points and ESETT
V3-018.q: When does a seizure become status epilepticus, and what did ESETT show about second-line drugs?
a: **ILAE 2015**: convulsive SE once a seizure lasts beyond **t1 = 5 min** (start treatment); lasting neuronal harm is likely beyond **t2 = 30 min**.
Why speed matters: as seizures continue, GABA-A receptors are internalised, so benzodiazepines lose effect; NMDA receptors increase, so excitation builds.
**ESETT** (Kapur, NEJM 2019): 400 enrolments, age ≥2, convulsive SE still seizing 5–30 min after an adequate benzodiazepine.
Arms over 10 min: levetiracetam **60 mg/kg** (max 4.5 g), fosphenytoin **20 mg PE/kg** (max 1.5 g), valproate **40 mg/kg** (max 3 g).
Primary outcome (seizures stopped and responsiveness improving at 60 min, no extra drug): **47%, 45%, 46%**. Stopped early for futility: no drug is better.
Safety similar: hypotension (0.7%, 3.2%, 1.6%) and intubation (20%, 26%, 17%) not significantly different. Choose by patient: avoid valproate in liver disease and pregnancy.
About half fail second line, so prepare intubation and an infusion while the second drug runs.
V3-018.src: Trinka E et al., ILAE definition of SE, Epilepsia 2015;56:1515; Kapur J et al., NEJM 2019;381:2103 (ESETT); Glauser T et al., AES guideline, Epilepsy Curr 2016;16:48

V3-019.topic: Refractory SE: anaesthetic infusions and EEG goals
V3-019.q: Status epilepticus continues after a benzodiazepine and a second-line drug. What now?
a: **Refractory SE**: seizures continue despite an adequate benzodiazepine and one adequate second-line drug. **Super-refractory**: continues or recurs **≥24 h** after anaesthetic therapy starts.
Intubate and ventilate; start **continuous EEG** (within 1 h if seizures may be ongoing, NCS 2012); hunt the cause: glucose, Na, Ca, Mg, toxins, CNS infection, autoimmune.
**Midazolam**: 0.2 mg/kg load, then 0.05–2 mg/kg/h. **Propofol**: 1–2 mg/kg, then 20–200 µg/kg/min; beware propofol infusion syndrome at high doses for long periods.
**Pentobarbital**: 5–15 mg/kg load, then 0.5–5 mg/kg/h; thiopentone is the usual Indian barbiturate. Expect hypotension needing pressors, ileus and a long washout.
Titrate to **cessation of electrographic seizures or burst suppression**; keep **24–48 h** of EEG control, then wean slowly.
Keep the second-line drug going at maintenance dose. Ketamine (NMDA antagonist) is a common add-on once benzodiazepines fail.
Super-refractory options: ketamine, inhaled anaesthetics, immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange), ketogenic diet, hypothermia, epilepsy surgery (SC-E-17).
V3-019.src: Brophy GM et al., NCS guideline for SE, Neurocrit Care 2012;17:3; Glauser T et al., AES guideline, Epilepsy Curr 2016;16:48

V3-020.topic: MgSO4 in eclampsia: Pritchard vs Zuspan, stop rules, antidote
V3-020.q: Give the Pritchard and Zuspan magnesium regimens, the checks before each dose, and the antidote.
a: **Pritchard (IM)**: 4 g IV of 20% slowly (about 5 min) **plus** 10 g IM of 50% (5 g deep in each buttock); then **5 g IM every 4 h** in alternate buttocks. Needs no pump; widely used in India.
**Zuspan (IV)**: 4 g IV over 5–15 min, then **1 g/h** infusion (the WHO IV regimen). The higher-dose US regimen gives 4–6 g, then 1–2 g/h.
Recurrent seizure on magnesium: a further **2 g IV** over 5 min. Continue for **24 h after delivery or the last seizure**, whichever is later.
**Before each dose and hourly**: patellar reflex present, **RR ≥16/min** (WHO; ≥12 in US protocols), urine **≥25–30 mL/h** (≥100 mL in 4 h).
A check fails: withhold the next IM dose or reduce the infusion and check a level. Oliguria is the usual cause: magnesium leaves only through the kidney.
Respiratory depression or arrest: stop magnesium, support ventilation, give **calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) slow IV over about 10 min**.
Therapeutic level **4–7 mEq/L** (2–3.5 mmol/L). Measure in renal impairment, absent reflexes or recurrent seizures.
V3-020.src: WHO, Managing complications in pregnancy and childbirth (MCPC), 2nd ed. 2017; WHO PQ magnesium sulfate product information (RH062); Pritchard JA, Surg Gynecol Obstet 1955;100:131; Zuspan FP, Clin Obstet Gynecol 1966;9:954; ACOG Practice Bulletin 222, Obstet Gynecol 2020

V3-021.topic: Hyponatraemia in brain injury: why not fluid-restrict
V3-021.q: A head-injured patient's sodium is falling. Why is hyponatraemia dangerous in brain injury, and why is fluid restriction risky?
a: Low sodium makes plasma hypotonic, so water moves into brain cells: oedema and ICP rise. A swollen brain has little compliance left, so even a **mild** fall matters.
Fluid restriction shrinks the circulating volume: MAP falls, so **CPP = MAP − ICP** falls. If the cause is cerebral salt wasting, restriction deepens the hypovolaemia.
Wijdicks 1985 (ruptured aneurysm): most hyponatraemic patients were **volume depleted**, not SIADH, and fluid restriction was linked to **cerebral infarction**.
So in brain injury: no hypotonic fluids (no 5% dextrose or 0.45% saline); 0.9% saline for maintenance; aim for euvolaemia.
Moderately severe or severe symptoms, or raised ICP: **3% saline 150 mL over 20 min**, repeated until sodium rises by **5 mmol/L** (European 2014).
Then treat by volume: hypovolaemic CSW → isotonic saline, salt, ± fludrocortisone. Euvolaemic SIADH → salt or urea; restrict only if CPP is safe. No vaptan with CNS symptoms.
Limit the rise to **10 mmol/L in the first 24 h** and 8 per day after. Acute hyponatraemia (under 48 h) carries less demyelination risk than chronic.
V3-021.src: Spasovski G et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1 (European hyponatraemia guideline); Verbalis JG et al., Am J Med 2013;126:S1; Wijdicks EFM et al., Ann Neurol 1985;17:137; Maesaka JK et al., Front Med 2018;5:319

V3-022.topic: SIADH vs cerebral salt wasting vs diabetes insipidus
V3-022.q: Differentiate SIADH, cerebral salt wasting and central diabetes insipidus.
a: Feature | **SIADH** | **CSW** | **CENTRAL DI**
Serum sodium | **Low** | **Low** | **High** (over 145)
Volume | Normal or slightly expanded | **Reduced**: negative balance | Reduced if water not replaced
Urine output | Normal or low | **High** | **Very high**: over 250 mL/h for 2 h; over 3–3.5 L/day
Urine | Concentrated; sodium over 30 | Concentrated; sodium over 30, often very high | **Dilute**: osmolality under 300, SG under 1.005
Urate excretion after sodium corrected | Normalises | **Stays high** (FEurate over 11%) | Not useful
Treatment | Fluid restriction (not in SAH or TBI); urea or salt | **Isotonic saline**, salt, fludrocortisone | **Desmopressin 1–2 µg IV/SC** + free water
Rule: SIADH and CSW share the same low sodium and salty urine, so **volume status** decides restriction vs saline. DI is the opposite problem: water lost, sodium high.
V3-022.src: Maesaka JK et al., Front Med 2018;5:319; Lamas C et al., Endocrinol Nutr 2014;61:e15; Maggiore U et al., Crit Care 2009;13:R110 (citing Agha criteria); Spasovski G et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1

V3-023.topic: SALSA trial: 3% saline boluses vs slow infusion
V3-023.q: What did the SALSA trial compare and show, and how does it fit the correction-rate debate?
a: **SALSA** (Baek, JAMA Intern Med 2021): open-label RCT, 3 Korean hospitals, **178** adults with moderately severe or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (sodium ≤125; mean 118).
Arms: 3% saline as **rapid intermittent boluses** vs **slow continuous infusion**, over 24–48 h.
Overcorrection: **17.2% vs 24.2%** (p = 0.26): no difference.
Boluses needed **less relowering** (41.4% vs 57.1%, p = 0.04) and reached the 1-hour target more often (32.2% vs 17.6%, intention to treat). Symptom relief did not differ.
Meaning: boluses are at least as safe as a drip and act faster, which supports the guideline bolus approach.
Debate: in large cohorts ODS was rare (**0.05%**, MacMillan 2023), and slower correction was linked to higher mortality (Seethapathy 2023). Keep the limits for high-risk patients.
V3-023.src: Baek SH et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021;181:81 (SALSA); MacMillan TE et al., NEJM Evid 2023;2(4); Seethapathy H et al., NEJM Evid 2023;2(10); Ayus JC et al., JAMA Intern Med 2025;185:38

V3-024.topic: Desmopressin clamp: proactive, reactive and rescue
V3-024.q: How is desmopressin used to prevent or reverse overcorrection of hyponatraemia?
a: Why: the danger is a sudden **water diuresis** once the cause resolves (volume restored, drug stopped, cortisol replaced). Desmopressin shuts that off, so the saline sets the rise.

**Proactive (clamp)**: desmopressin **1–2 µg IV or SC every 6–8 h** from the start, with 3% saline dosed to the target rise. Sood 2013: 25 patients, rise **5.8** mmol/L on day 1, none over 12 in 24 h.
**Reactive**: give desmopressin when sodium is rising too fast or dilute urine starts to pour, to stop further rise.
**Rescue**: once the limit is crossed, desmopressin plus electrolyte-free water to re-lower (NA-16).
Evidence is small: AlShanableh 2025 (cohort, 184 patients) overcorrection **6.8% vs 27.1%** proactive vs reactive; Pakchotanon 2024 RCT (49 patients) 16.7% vs 28%, not significant (p = 0.54).
Caution: on a clamp any free water drops sodium further, so control intake strictly and check sodium often. Guidelines do not mandate a routine clamp.
V3-024.src: Sood L et al., Am J Kidney Dis 2013;61:571; Sterns RH, Hix JK, Silver SM, Chest 2013;144:672; AlShanableh Z et al., Kidney360 2025;6:1462; Pakchotanon K et al., Sci Rep 2024;14:7487; Spasovski G et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1

V3-025.topic: Hypernatraemia and central DI after brain injury
V3-025.q: How do you manage hypernatraemia in brain injury, and how do you diagnose and treat central diabetes insipidus?
a: Two kinds: **deliberate** (osmotherapy, sodium kept about 145–155) and **unwanted** (central DI or a free-water deficit). Hypernatraemia after severe TBI is linked to higher mortality.
Suspect central DI: urine over **250 mL/h for 2 h** without mannitol or diuretic, dilute urine (osmolality under 300, SG under 1.005), sodium over **145** and rising.
Criteria used after TBI (Agha): sodium over 145, polyuria over **3.5 L/day**, urine osmolality under 300. Early DI often marks severe injury, herniation or coming brain death.
Treat: replace losses with free water (enteral water or IV dextrose) and give **desmopressin 1–2 µg IV or SC**; it lasts 6–12 h, so repeat when polyuria returns.
Triphasic response (stalk or hypothalamic injury): **1** DI for about 5–7 days → **2** SIADH-like antidiuresis for 2–14 days as stored ADH leaks out → **3** permanent DI.
Phase 2 trap: continued desmopressin or free water now causes **hyponatraemia**. Stop desmopressin, restrict water, check sodium every 6–8 h.

Lower chronic hypernatraemia by about **0.5 mmol/L/h**, no more than **10–12 per day** (Adrogué 2000). With raised ICP avoid a fast fall (rebound oedema); NCS 2020 sets no rate but warns about sudden sodium shifts.
V3-025.src: Maggiore U et al., Crit Care 2009;13:R110; Lamas C et al., Endocrinol Nutr 2014;61:e15 (SEEN guideline, DI after pituitary surgery); Karali V et al., Crit Care 2008;12(Suppl 2):P130; Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, NEJM 2000;342:1493; Cook AM et al., Neurocrit Care 2020;32:647 (NCS cerebral oedema guideline)

V3-026.topic: Reading a CT head for subarachnoid haemorrhage
V3-026.q: Spotter: non-contrast CT head showing subarachnoid haemorrhage. What do you describe, and how do you grade it?
a: Name it: **hyperdense** blood in the subarachnoid spaces: basal cisterns (the suprasellar star), sylvian fissures, interhemispheric fissure, cortical sulci.
Where the blood is thickest hints at the aneurysm: interhemispheric fissure → **ACom**; sylvian fissure → **MCA**; prepontine cistern and fourth ventricle → posterior circulation.
Blood only in the cisterns in front of the midbrain and pons, with a normal angiogram = **perimesencephalic** (non-aneurysmal) SAH, with a benign course.
Then the complications: **IVH** (blood layering in the occipital horns), **hydrocephalus** (dilated temporal horns), parenchymal clot, oedema, midline shift.
Grade it on **modified Fisher** (Frontera 2006): thin vs thick cisternal blood, with or without IVH. Symptomatic vasospasm about 24%, 33%, 33% and **40%** for grades 1–4.
Close with the plan: CTA for the aneurysm, EVD if hydrocephalus, nimodipine, early securing.
V3-026.src: Frontera JA et al., Neurosurgery 2006;59:21 (modified Fisher scale); Hoh BL et al., AHA/ASA aSAH guideline, Stroke 2023;54:e314

V3-027.topic: Stroke reperfusion: tenecteplase and thrombectomy windows
V3-027.q: Acute ischaemic stroke: what are the thrombolysis and thrombectomy windows, and what is the tenecteplase dose?
a: IV lysis within **4.5 h** of last known well, disabling deficit (any NIHSS), no bleed on CT: **alteplase 0.9 mg/kg** (max 90 mg) or **tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg** (max 25 mg) as one bolus. TNK 0.4 mg/kg is not recommended.
Tenecteplase: non-inferior to alteplase (AcT, Lancet 2022); better reperfusion before thrombectomy (EXTEND-IA TNK, NEJM 2018). One bolus suits transfer.
Unknown onset, wake-up or **4.5–9 h**: lysis only if imaging shows salvageable brain: MRI DWI–FLAIR mismatch (WAKE-UP, NEJM 2018) or perfusion mismatch (AHA/ASA 2026).
Thrombectomy, ICA or M1 occlusion, NIHSS ≥6, prestroke mRS 0–1: within **6 h** if ASPECTS **3–10**, even after lysis. Do not delay lysis for CTA or perfusion imaging.
**6–16 h**: DEFUSE-3 perfusion criteria (core under 70 mL, mismatch ratio ≥1.8, penumbra ≥15 mL; n = 182): mRS 0–2 at 90 days **45% vs 17%**.
**6–24 h**: DAWN clinical–core mismatch (small core, NIHSS ≥10; n = 206): functional independence at 90 days **49% vs 13%**.
Large core (AHA/ASA 2026): ICA or M1, age under 80, NIHSS ≥6, ASPECTS **3–5**, no mass effect: EVT up to **24 h** (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, RESCUE-Japan LIMIT). ASPECTS 0–2 within 6 h: reasonable.
Basilar occlusion: EVT within **24 h** if NIHSS ≥10, prestroke mRS 0–1, PC-ASPECTS ≥6. After successful EVT, pushing SBP under **140** is harmful.
V3-027.src: Prabhakaran S et al., 2026 AHA/ASA guideline for early management of AIS, Stroke 2026 (doi 10.1161/STR.0000000000000513; replaces Powers 2019); Menon BK et al., Lancet 2022;400:161 (AcT); Campbell BCV et al., NEJM 2018;378:1573 (EXTEND-IA TNK); Thomalla G et al., NEJM 2018;379:611 (WAKE-UP); Albers GW et al., NEJM 2018;378:708 (DEFUSE 3); Nogueira RG et al., NEJM 2018;378:11 (DAWN); Yoshimura S et al., NEJM 2022;386:1303; Sarraj A et al., NEJM 2023;388:1259; Huo X et al., NEJM 2023;388:1272

V3-028.topic: Tetanus: mechanism, forms and Ablett grading
V3-028.q: What happens in tetanus, and how do you grade its severity?
a: **Tetanospasmin** from *C. tetani* in a wound travels up motor nerves and stops inhibitory interneurons releasing **GABA and glycine**: the motor neurons and sympathetic outflow fire unchecked.
Result: **rigidity** (trismus first), **reflex spasms** and **autonomic overactivity**. Consciousness is preserved, so spasms are painful.
Forms: **generalised** (commonest), **localised** (near the wound), **cephalic** (head wounds, cranial nerves) and **neonatal**.
**ABLETT GRADE** | **FEATURES**
**I (mild)** | Mild–moderate trismus, spasticity; no spasms, no respiratory compromise, little dysphagia
**II (moderate)** | Moderate trismus, marked rigidity, short spasms; RR **>30**; mild dysphagia
**III (severe)** | Severe trismus, prolonged reflex spasms; RR **>40**, apnoeic spells, severe dysphagia; HR **>120**
**IV (very severe)** | Grade III plus **violent autonomic swings**: hypertension and tachycardia alternating with hypotension and bradycardia
V3-028.src: Ablett JJL 1967 (classification), as tabulated in Int J Emerg Med 2021 (s12245-021-00346-9); CDC Clinical Care of Tetanus

V3-029.topic: Tetanus: wound, antitoxin, antibiotic and vaccine
V3-029.q: How do you stop the toxin in tetanus: wound care, antitoxin dose, antibiotic and vaccination?
a: **Wound**: clean, debride necrotic tissue, remove foreign material. The wound is the toxin factory.
**Human tetanus immunoglobulin (HTIG)**: a **single IM dose** as soon as possible (WHO 2017). CDC: **500 IU** IM is as effective as the older **3000–6000 IU**, with less pain.
Antitoxin neutralises only **unbound** toxin; toxin already inside nerves is untouched, so it does not reverse established signs. Infiltrating part around the wound is unproven.
No HTIG: **equine antitoxin**, one large dose after a sensitivity test (WHO). Van Hao 2022: equine **21,000 IU** IM was as good as human 3000 IU (ventilation 44% vs 45%).

**Antibiotic**: WHO prefers **metronidazole or penicillin G**; IV metronidazole is **500 mg 6-hourly**. Ahmadsyah 1985 (n = 173, non-randomised): metronidazole had lower mortality and shorter stay than procaine penicillin.
But Ganesh Kumar 2004 (India, RCT, n = 161): oral metronidazole 600 mg 6-hourly × 10 days = benzathine or IV benzylpenicillin. Metronidazole is favoured; penicillin is acceptable.
**Vaccinate**: the disease gives **no immunity**. Start or complete tetanus toxoid once the patient is stable.
V3-029.src: WHO Tetanus vaccines position paper, Wkly Epidemiol Rec 2017;92(6):53; CDC Clinical Care of Tetanus (web page); Van Hao N et al., Lancet Glob Health 2022;10:e862; Ahmadsyah I et al., BMJ 1985;291:648; Ganesh Kumar AV et al., Ann Trop Med Parasitol 2004;98:59; Karnad DR, Gupta V, Indian J Crit Care Med 2021;25(Suppl 2):S155

V3-030.topic: Tetanus: spasms, autonomic storm and magnesium
V3-030.q: How do you control spasms and autonomic instability in tetanus, and what did the magnesium trial show?
a: **Spasms**: benzodiazepines first (diazepam; Cochrane in children, death RR **0.36** vs phenobarbitone plus chlorpromazine). Dark, quiet room; minimal handling.
Refractory spasms or laryngospasm: **neuromuscular blocker and ventilation**. Ventilation runs weeks (median about **16 days** in Van Hao 2022): plan a tracheostomy.
**Thwaites, Lancet 2006** (Vietnam): **195** severe tetanus patients, magnesium vs placebo infusion for 7 days. Need for ventilation not reduced: **OR 0.71 (0.36–1.40)**.
But magnesium cut the doses of **midazolam and pipecuronium**, and patients were **4.7 times** less likely to need **verapamil** for cardiovascular instability. Survival was the same.

Rodrigo 2012 meta-analysis (**3 trials, 275** patients): **no fall in mortality** (vs placebo RR **0.80, 0.41–1.58**). Use it to spare sedatives and calm the autonomic storm, not to avoid the ventilator.
Regimens: Thwaites 2006 **40 mg/kg over 30 min**, then **2 g/h**; Attygalle 1997 **5 g** load, then **2–3 g/h** to spasms. Target **2–4 mmol/L** (4–8 mEq/L); keep the **patellar reflex present**.

Autonomic storm: short-acting agents only: labetalol, esmolol, clonidine, morphine, dexmedetomidine; each has only small series behind it. **No long-acting β-blockers**: the storm can flip to bradycardia, hypotension and asystole.
V3-030.src: Thwaites CL et al., Lancet 2006;368:1436 (ISRCTN74651862); Rodrigo C et al., Anaesthesia 2012;67:1370; Rodrigo C, Fernando D, Rajapakse S, Crit Care 2014;18:217; Attygalle D, Rodrigo N, Anaesthesia 1997;52:956; Karnad DR, Gupta V, Indian J Crit Care Med 2021;25(Suppl 2):S155; Okoromah CN, Lesi FE, Cochrane review (diazepam for neonatal tetanus), as cited in Rodrigo 2014

V3-031.q: Should antitetanus immunoglobulin be given intrathecally? Give the evidence.
a: Why try it: the toxin acts **inside the CNS**, and IM antitoxin crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly.

**Kabura 2006** meta-analysis (Trop Med Int Health): **12 trials, 942 patients**: intrathecal cut mortality, **RR 0.71 (0.62–0.81)**. But most trials were weak: only **two** concealed allocation, and safety was rarely reported.

**Agarwal 1998** (CMC Vellore, Natl Med J India): **36** adults, **250 IU** intrathecal vs sham. In mild tetanus: slower progression, shorter ICU and hospital stay, fewer tracheostomies; mortality 20% vs 30%.

**Miranda-Filho 2004** (BMJ, Brazil ICU): **120** patients, **1000 IU** intrathecal plus 3000 IU IM vs IM alone. Better clinical progression, shorter spasms and respiratory support; deaths 4 vs 10, NS.
**Van Hao 2022** (Lancet Glob Health, Vietnam, 2×2, **272** adults): **500 IU** intrathecal vs sham. Ventilation **43% vs 50%, RR 0.87 (0.66–1.13)**, NS. Safe, no deaths from the procedure.
Verdict: intrathecal is **safe but unproven** where ventilation is available. Standard care is **IM** antitoxin; US preparations are not licensed for intrathecal use.
If used, it must be a **preservative-free** product, within a trial or local protocol.
V3-031.src: Kabura L et al., Trop Med Int Health 2006;11:1075 (figures as cited in Van Hao 2022); Agarwal M et al., Natl Med J India 1998;11:209; Miranda-Filho DB et al., BMJ 2004;328:615; Van Hao N et al., Lancet Glob Health 2022;10:e862; CDC Clinical Care of Tetanus

questions.text: Case: fever and altered sensorium. What will you do with the CSF in an ABG machine?

steps.bridge: Fever plus altered sensorium has a short list, and infection leads it. Next: what the CSF must be sent for →
Culture is the gold standard but slow, and neutrophils fall within an hour. Next: the patterns that separate the causes →
Neutrophils and glucose below 40% say bacterial. Next: how well CSF lactate separates bacterial from aseptic →
Lactate is 93% sensitive and 96% specific, but halves after antibiotics. Next: where CSF lactate comes from →
Lysis drives cytokines, low cerebral flow and ischaemia. Next: running the CSF on the blood-gas analyser and reading it →

spine: Present: fever with altered sensorium is meningitis or encephalitis until proved otherwise; I also think of cerebral malaria and septic encephalopathy.
What I do: blood cultures, LP at once if no CT criterion, dexamethasone and antibiotics within the hour; fresh CSF straight into the ICU blood-gas analyser for lactate and glucose.
Reading it: CSF lactate **>3.5 mmol/L** favours bacterial. The meta-analysis optimum is **35 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L)**: sensitivity **93%**, specificity **96%**.
Why it is high: it is made inside the CNS, by ischaemic brain (low flow, vasculitis, raised ICP) through anaerobic glycolysis, and by neutrophils and bacteria. Not from blood.
Caution: after antibiotics sensitivity falls to **49%**; a bloody tap, delay, seizures or neurosurgery raise it. It supports Gram stain, culture and PCR, never replaces them.

questions.text: Bacterial vs viral vs TB meningitis — how do you differentiate?

steps.bridge: Bacterial is cloudy with over 1000 cells; viral is gin-clear. Next: the differential, glucose and protein →
Neutrophils mean bacterial; TB has the lowest glucose and highest protein. Next: real numbers from a bacterial vs non-bacterial series →
Procalcitonin and the glucose ratio separate the groups best. Next: how CSF lactate performs →
The optimal lactate cut-off is about 35 mg/dL. Next: the same cut-off in mmol/L, and why lactate rises →

spine: What it is: cells, CSF:blood glucose ratio and protein separate the three; lactate, ADA and PCR sharpen it.
Bacterial: cloudy, often **>1000** cells, neutrophils, glucose ratio **<0.4**, protein **>1 g/L**.
Viral: clear, lymphocytes, normal glucose, protein normal or mildly raised. TB: lymphocytes under 500, glucose very low (**<0.3**), protein 1–5 g/L, ADA and GeneXpert.
Lactate: **>3.5 mmol/L** favours bacterial; the meta-analysis optimum is **35 mg/dL, about 3.9 mmol/L** (Sakushima 2011: sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.96).
Caution: early viral and partly treated bacterial overlap; after antibiotics lactate sensitivity is only **0.49**. CMV and early TB can mimic bacterial.

questions.text: What is the role of CT in meningitis, and what are the findings?

steps.bridge: CT before LP is a herniation screen, and only a few need it. Next: what CT and MRI each show →
CT is the quick screen; MRI with gadolinium is the imaging of choice. Next: the patterns that point to TB, HSV or JE →
TB is basal, HSV temporal, JE thalamic. Next: the three guidelines compared, the evidence for prompt LP, and the CT findings →

spine: What it is: CT before LP is a safety screen for shift or swelling that would make LP cause herniation. Most patients do not need it.
When: UK 2016: focal signs, papilloedema, uncontrolled seizures, **GCS ≤12**. ESCMID 2016: focal deficit, new seizures, severe immunocompromise, **GCS <10**.
Can I do LP without CT: yes, if none apply. Glimåker 2018: prompt LP had lower mortality than CT first (adjusted OR **0.38**).
What I do: if CT is needed, blood cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics go in first, then the scan, then the LP.
Findings: often normal; oedema, hydrocephalus, infarcts, cerebritis or abscess, subdural empyema, meningeal enhancement, and a sinus or mastoid source. MRI is better.

questions.text: How do you treat community-acquired meningitis?

steps.bridge: The organism follows age, and Listeria sits at both extremes. Next: the drug and dose for each organism →
Cephalosporins cover all but Listeria, which needs amoxicillin. Next: how this becomes one empirical regimen →
Ceftriaxone, vancomycin if resistance, ampicillin if Listeria risk. Next: the steroid that goes in with the first dose →
Dexamethasone goes with or before the first antibiotic. Next: how long to treat once the organism is known →

spine: What I do: blood cultures, then dexamethasone 10 mg and antibiotics at once. I never wait for CT or LP.
Regimen: ceftriaxone **2 g 12-hourly** (or cefotaxime 2 g 4–6-hourly), plus vancomycin where resistant pneumococcus is possible.
Ampicillin **2 g 4-hourly** for Listeria if age **>50**, pregnant, immunosuppressed, alcoholic, diabetic or with cancer: cephalosporins never cover Listeria.
If encephalitis is possible (seizures, focal signs, behaviour change), I add aciclovir **10 mg/kg 8-hourly** until the HSV PCR returns.
Then narrow: meningococcus **7 days**, pneumococcus **10–14**, Listeria **at least 21**; dexamethasone 4 days, continued only if pneumococcal (IDSA).

questions.text: Dexamethasone in meningitis — when?

steps.bridge: Bacterial lysis releases cell-wall products that drive the cytokine surge. Next: the steroid dose and timing that blunt it →
Dexamethasone 4 days, with or before the first antibiotic. Next: the trial behind it, the window and when to stop →

spine: What: dexamethasone **0.15 mg/kg (10 mg) 6-hourly for 4 days**, started 15–20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic.
Why: it blunts the cytokine surge from antibiotic-induced bacterial lysis, so it must be on board before or with that lysis.
Evidence: de Gans 2002, 301 adults: unfavourable outcome **15% vs 25%**, death **7% vs 15%**; in pneumococcal meningitis death **14% vs 34%**.
Antibiotics already in: ESCMID allows a start up to **4 h** after the first dose, not later. IDSA says do not start; UK 2016 allows up to 12 h.
Stop or continue: 4 days if pneumococcal (IDSA), or pneumococcal or H. influenzae (ESCMID); consider stopping for others, stop for **Listeria** or if not bacterial.

questions.text: What is the role of steroids in tuberculous meningitis?

steps.bridge: TB meningitis is a basal exudate with hydrocephalus and infarcts. Next: the drugs and the steroid dose →
2HRZE then HR, with dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/day tapered. Next: the two trials, HIV-negative and HIV-positive →

spine: What: dexamethasone about **0.4 mg/kg/day**, tapered over **6–8 weeks** (WHO; ICMR 8–12), alongside 2 months HRZE then HR (HRE in NTEP). WHO: strong recommendation.
Why: thick basal exudate causes hydrocephalus, vasculitic infarcts and cranial nerve palsies; steroids damp that inflammation.
HIV-negative: Thwaites 2004, 545 patients in Vietnam: 9-month death **31.8% vs 41.3%** (RR **0.69**), but no fewer severely disabled survivors.
ACT HIV (Donovan, NEJM 2023), 520 HIV-positive adults: 12-month death **44.1% vs 49.0%**, HR **0.85** (0.66–1.10), p = 0.22: no survival benefit.
So: every HIV-negative patient gets it. In HIV the benefit is unproven, so I weigh it case by case; WHO still recommends steroids in all TB meningitis.

questions.text: How do you treat viral meningitis / encephalitis?

steps.bridge: Enteroviruses cause most aseptic meningitis, which is self-limiting. Next: what tells you the brain itself is involved →
Encephalitis is parenchymal: disorientation, speech and behaviour change, seizures. Next: where HSV shows on MRI →
HSV is temporal and orbitofrontal, bilateral but asymmetrical. Next: the aciclovir dose and duration →
10 mg/kg 8-hourly, 14 or 21 days, repeat LP at the end. Next: what the outcome is even with treatment →
Only 14% recover fully, so time matters. Next: why you start aciclovir before any result →

spine: Viral meningitis: usually enterovirus and self-limiting; supportive care with analgesia, antipyretics and fluids.
Encephalitis (altered sensorium, seizures, focal signs): IV aciclovir **10 mg/kg 8-hourly** at once, before HSV PCR or MRI returns (IDSA 2008).
Why urgent: treated HSV encephalitis still had **28%** mortality at 18 months, and **8%** when aciclovir started within 4 days of onset.
Duration: **14–21 days**; 14 if immunocompetent, 21 if immunocompromised; repeat LP and continue if the PCR is still positive.
Caution: early PCR can be falsely negative, so repeat it in **3–7 days** before stopping. Adjust to renal function and hydrate well against crystal nephropathy.

questions.text: What is the GCS and the FOUR score - which is better in the ICU?

steps.bridge: GCS adds eye 1–4, verbal 1–5 and motor 1–6 for a total of 3–15. Next: what happens to it once the patient is intubated →
Intubated means verbal is untestable, so GCS can only record VT. Next: when to score it and how it grades TBI →
Score after resuscitation, before sedation; 3–8 is severe TBI. Next: the scale built for the intubated, comatose patient →

spine: What it is: GCS is eye, verbal and motor, **3–15**. FOUR (Wijdicks 2005) is eye, motor, brainstem and respiration, each 0–4, total **0–16**.
Why FOUR in the ICU: it has **no verbal part**, so an intubated patient gets a full score; GCS can only write VT.
It adds what GCS misses: pupils, corneals and cough, the breathing pattern, and eye tracking or blinking to command, which detects **locked-in syndrome**.
Evidence: validated in **120 ICU patients**, inter-rater agreement as good as GCS (κ **0.82**); it splits the GCS-3 group and its lowest totals carried higher mortality.
What I do: GCS stays the language of TBI guidelines, triage and trials, so I record both. I follow the intubated or comatose patient with FOUR.
Caution: score GCS after resuscitation and before sedation or paralysis. FOUR 0 means no brainstem reflexes or breathing: exclude confounders and consider formal brain death testing.

questions.text: ICP monitoring indications in TBI — abnormal vs normal CT.

steps.bridge: Clinical signs of high ICP come late; a monitor guides CPP and drainage. Next: which TBI patients need one →
Severe TBI with abnormal CT, or normal CT with 2 of age >40, posturing, SBP <90. Next: indications beyond TBI and when not to →
ICP monitors also serve ICH, SAH, hydrocephalus and liver failure; coagulopathy limits them. Next: what number you treat →
BTF 4th: treat ICP above 22 mmHg, read with clinical and CT findings. Next: the CPP that goes with it →
CPP 60–70 mmHg, with no aggressive push above 70. Next: the whole answer as one worked question →

spine: Who: severe TBI, **GCS 3–8** after resuscitation, salvageable, with an **abnormal CT** (haematoma, contusion, swelling, herniation or compressed cisterns).
Normal CT: monitor if **≥2 of 3**: age **>40**, uni- or bilateral motor posturing, SBP **<90 mmHg**. These come from the 3rd edition, Level III (Narayan 1982).
What I treat: BTF 4th ed. (2016), treat ICP **>22 mmHg** (Level IIB), together with the clinical picture and CT, and keep CPP **60–70 mmHg**.
Evidence: the 4th edition says only that managing severe TBI with ICP data lowers in-hospital and 2-week mortality. BEST-TRIP (2012) found ICP-guided care no better than imaging plus exam.
Caution: a normal CT does not rule out monitoring. Coagulopathy is the main practical contraindication; the EVD is the gold standard and also drains CSF.

questions.text: What does ONSD tell you?

steps.bridge: The orbital sheath fills with CSF under pressure; measure 3 mm behind the globe, cut-off about 5–5.9 mm. Next: how it ranks among non-invasive tools →

spine: Spot: linear probe on the closed eyelid; the optic nerve sheath measured **3 mm behind the globe**.
Why it works: the subarachnoid space around the optic nerve is continuous with intracranial CSF, so a raised ICP distends the sheath.
Cut-off: about **5.0–5.9 mm** across studies. Higher cut-offs (about **5.6–6.3 mm**) are more specific for raised ICP.
Evidence: meta-analyses give sensitivity about **0.90** and specificity about **0.85** against invasive ICP.
Caution: it screens, it does not give a number, and it is not a replacement for an invasive monitor. Optic neuritis, trauma or an orbital mass also widen the sheath.

questions.text: Spotter - ICP waveform. What does it show?

steps.bridge: ICP is 5–15 mmHg; the pressure-volume curve turns steep once reserve is spent. Next: how each pulse shows that reserve →
P1 is the arterial pulse, P2 brain compliance, P3 the dicrotic notch; P2 above P1 means a stiff brain. Next: the exam version with traps →
P2 above P1 warns even before the mean ICP is high; a damped trace is a line fault. Next: the slow waves on the trend →
A plateau waves (50–100 for 5–20 min) are always bad; C waves are physiological. Next: check yourself on the traps →

spine: Spot: an ICP pulse waveform with three peaks. **P1** percussion (arterial pulse via choroid plexus), **P2** tidal (brain compliance), **P3** dicrotic (aortic valve closure).
Normal: **P1 > P2 > P3**, a descending staircase.
Here: **P2 taller than P1** means intracranial compliance is exhausted. We are on the steep part of the pressure-volume curve, even if the mean ICP is not yet high.
Mechanism: once CSF and venous blood have been displaced, each arterial pulse makes a bigger pressure rise in the brain itself, so the tidal wave grows.
What I do: act before the number climbs. Head up, sedation, CO₂ in range, osmotherapy or CSF drainage; look on the trend for Lundberg A plateau waves (**50–100 mmHg**, 5–20 min).
Caution: a damped, rounded trace with lost peaks is air or a blocked catheter, not a good reading. Flush or re-zero first.

questions.text: What is the CPP target and what is cerebral autoregulation?

steps.bridge: CPP is MAP minus ICP; autoregulation holds flow steady over MAP 50–150, and injury breaks it. Next: what the guideline sets as the target →
BTF: CPP 60–70 mmHg; forcing it above 70 is discouraged. Next: where CPP and the MAP challenge sit in the escalation ladder →
SIBICC uses CPP 60–70 in Tier 1 and a MAP challenge in Tier 2. Next: how PRx finds each patient's own best CPP →

spine: What it is: CPP = MAP − ICP. BTF 4th ed. target **60–70 mmHg** (Level IIB); below 60 risks ischaemia, and pushing above 70 with fluid and pressors risks ARDS.
Autoregulation: arterioles constrict or dilate to keep cerebral blood flow steady over a plateau, classically **MAP 50–150**. After injury it narrows, shifts right or is lost.
Individualise: **PRx** is a moving correlation of slow MAP and ICP waves. Near zero or negative = intact; above about **0.2–0.3** = impaired. PRx >0.25 was linked to death.
CPPopt: plot PRx against CPP; the bottom of the U is the patient's optimal CPP (Steiner 2002). **COGiTATE** (2021, 60 patients) showed targeting it is feasible and safe.
What I do: aim for 60–70; with PRx available, aim near CPPopt. Without it, a SIBICC MAP challenge: if ICP falls or stays flat as MAP rises, autoregulation is intact.
Caution: CPPopt is not yet outcome-proven; a phase III trial is still needed.

questions.text: How do you manage raised ICP in TBI — the tiers?

steps.bridge: A stiff box: once compensation is spent, small volumes give big ICP rises. Next: the thresholds that trigger treatment →
Treat ICP above 22 and hold CPP 60–70, with osmotherapy in bolus doses. Next: how SIBICC stacks the measures into tiers →
SIBICC climbs from Tier 0 basics to Tier 3 rescue only as each tier fails. Next: how this differs from the older ladder in your notes →
The older ladder hyperventilates early; SIBICC keeps PaCO2 35–38 in Tier 1. Next: the follow-up, mannitol or saline →
Both osmotic agents work; choose by volume status and sodium. Next: the Tier 3 drugs and what BTF says of them →
Barbiturates for refractory ICP only, never as prophylaxis. Next: the surgical Tier 3 option and its two trials →

spine: What it is: SIBICC 2019 is a tiered ladder for ICP above **22 mmHg**. Escalate only when the lower tier fails, and keep CPP **60–70**.
Tier 0: head up 30–45°, neutral neck, sedation and analgesia, SpO2 ≥94%, PaCO2 35–45, no fever, avoid low sodium, Hb >7.
Tier 1: deeper sedation, PaCO2 **35–38**, mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline boluses, CSF drainage by EVD, consider EEG.
Tier 2: mild hypocapnia **32–35**, paralysis, MAP challenge. Tier 3: barbiturate coma, secondary decompressive craniectomy, mild hypothermia **35–36 °C**.
Mannitol or saline: saline if hypotensive or hypovolaemic, mannitol if sodium is high. Boluses only. Limits: Na **155**, osmolality **320**.
Caution: no steroids, no routine PaCO2 <30, no CPP >90. DECRA: early DC worsened function; RESCUEicp: last-tier DC saved lives at the cost of disability.

questions.text: Mannitol or hypertonic saline for raised ICP?

steps.bridge: Both pull water from the brain; the doses and the switch rules are here. Next: how each agent actually works and what trials show →
Saline expands volume, mannitol diureses; NCS leans to saline, no outcome gain. Next: what the guideline base says →
BTF: both lower ICP, no evidence to pick one or claim outcome benefit. Next: how to monitor mannitol safely →
The osmolar gap tracks mannitol still in blood; redose when it falls. Next: how the gap is calculated →
Gap = measured minus calculated osmolality; mannitol is one unmeasured osmole. Next: the sodium and osmolality ceilings →

spine: What they share: both raise plasma osmolality and pull water from brain where the barrier is intact. Mannitol dose **0.25–1 g/kg** as a bolus.
Mechanism: mannitol first lowers blood viscosity, then pulls water, then causes a diuresis. Hypertonic saline stays in the vessels and expands volume.
Evidence: NCS 2020 suggests saline first for ICP in TBI, with mannitol an effective alternative. No trial shows better outcome; COBI continuous saline did not help.
What I do: hypotensive or bleeding patient gets saline; high sodium or chloride gets mannitol. Bolus for a rise, and keep Na at or below **155**.
Monitoring mannitol: check the **osmolar gap**, measured minus calculated, before each repeat dose; it tracks unmeasured mannitol. Redose when the trough is under about **20**.
Caution: a high gap goes with AKI, and repeated doses can leak into injured brain and cause rebound. Replace urine losses.

questions.text: Tell us about decompressive craniectomy trials.

steps.bridge: Primary DC is done with a clot evacuation; secondary DC treats raised ICP. Next: the outcome scale both trials used →
GOS-E runs 1–8; DECRA called 1–4 unfavourable, RESCUEicp counted upper severe disability (4) as favourable. Next: the two trials →
DECRA: early DC, same deaths, worse function; RESCUEicp: last-tier DC, fewer deaths, more disability. Next: why DECRA did worse →
Early trigger, bifrontal technique and a pupil imbalance explain DECRA. Next: what BTF now recommends →

spine: What it is: secondary decompressive craniectomy removes bone and opens dura for raised ICP. Two trials frame it: DECRA (early) and RESCUEicp (last tier).
DECRA 2011: 155 diffuse TBI, bifrontal DC for ICP **>20 for 15 min**. ICP fell, mortality the same (**19 vs 18%**), unfavourable outcome worse (**70 vs 51%**).
Why worse: trigger too early and too low, bifrontal without dividing the falx, and more unreactive pupils in the DC arm (**27 vs 12%**). Adjusted, significance was lost.
RESCUEicp 2016: 408 patients, ICP **>25 for 1–12 h** despite medical tiers. Deaths **26.9 vs 48.9%**, but more vegetative state (8.5 vs 2.1%) and severe disability.
At 12 months favourable outcome was **45.4 vs 32.4%**. DC trades death for dependency, so the family must hear that before consent.
What I do: DC as Tier 3 for refractory ICP, large frontotemporoparietal flap (at least 12 × 15 cm), not early bifrontal DC (BTF).

questions.text: Role of therapeutic hypothermia in TBI?

steps.bridge: Eurotherm cooled for high ICP and did harm; POLAR cooled early and did nothing. Next: why Eurotherm stopped, with the numbers →
Stopped by its monitoring committee for worse outcomes despite ICP control. Next: what BTF says of prophylactic cooling →
BTF IIB: no early prophylactic hypothermia in diffuse injury. Next: where mild cooling still sits in the ICP ladder →

spine: What it is: cooling lowers cerebral metabolism and ICP. Two uses were tested: cooling to treat high ICP (Eurotherm) and cooling to prevent injury (POLAR).
Eurotherm3235 2015: ICP >20 despite stage-1 therapy, cooled to **32–35 °C**. ICP was controlled with fewer stage-3 drugs, but outcome was worse: adjusted OR **1.53**.
Why stopped: the monitoring committee halted it at 387 of 600 because outcomes, including deaths (**34.9 vs 26.6%**), were worse with cooling.
POLAR 2018: 511 severe TBI, early prophylactic cooling to **33 °C** for at least 72 h. Favourable outcome **48.8 vs 49.1%**, with more pneumonia and bradycardia.
What I do: normothermia and aggressive fever control. Mild hypothermia **35–36 °C** only as a SIBICC Tier 3 rescue for refractory ICP.
Caution: a lower ICP number is not a better brain. BTF advises against prophylactic hypothermia.

questions.text: What is the transfusion threshold in brain injury?

steps.bridge: The general ICU trigger is 7 g/dL. Next: why the brain was thought to need more, first in SAH →
SAH guidance left 7–10 as a grey zone guided by brain oxygen. Next: the TBI trial, HEMOTION →
HEMOTION: transfusing at 10 leaned better but missed significance. Next: TRAIN and SAHaRA side by side →

spine: What it is: the general ICU trigger is Hb **7 g/dL**, but injured brain may need more oxygen delivery. Three trials tested a higher trigger in 2024–25.
TRAIN (JAMA 2024): 820 TBI, SAH or ICH; transfuse at **<9 vs <7**. Unfavourable outcome **62.6 vs 72.6%** (RR 0.86), with less cerebral ischaemia.
HEMOTION (NEJM 2024): 742 TBI, **≤10 vs ≤7**, **68.4 vs 73.5%**, not significant. SAHaRA (NEJM 2025): 742 SAH, **≤10 vs ≤8**, 33.5 vs 37.7%, not significant.
Did liberal help? It improved outcome in TRAIN only; the other two leaned the same way without significance. TRAIN and HEMOTION showed no safety signal.
What I do: in acute brain injury I do not wait for 7; I transfuse at about **9 g/dL**, sooner if PbtO2 is low or vasospasm is active.
Caution: each unit carries TACO, TRALI and infection risk, so I give single units and recheck.

questions.text: Spotter - CT head showing extradural vs subdural haematoma.

steps.bridge: EDH and SDH are both extra-axial, outside the brain. Next: how to tell them apart on CT →
Lens that stops at sutures is extradural; crescent that crosses sutures is subdural. Next: which ones go to theatre →
EDH over 30 mL, SDH over 10 mm or shift over 5 mm: operate at any GCS. Next: the imaging rules around the scan →

spine: Spot: a biconvex, lens-shaped hyperdensity that stops at sutures is **extradural**. A crescent that crosses sutures and hugs the hemisphere is **subdural**.
Mechanism: EDH is usually arterial, the middle meningeal artery under a temporal fracture, sometimes with a lucid interval. SDH comes from torn bridging veins.
Measure: thickness, midline shift, basal cisterns, contusions, and volume by **ABC/2**.
Surgery (BTF 2006): EDH **>30 mL** at any GCS, or any EDH in coma with anisocoria. Acute SDH **>10 mm** thick or shift **>5 mm** at any GCS.
Smaller lesions: watch EDH if <30 mL, <15 mm, shift <5 mm, GCS >8, no deficit. Small SDH in coma: operate if GCS falls by **2**, pupils change, or ICP is >20.
Caution: SDH has the worse prognosis because of injury beneath. Reverse anticoagulants, repeat CT for growth, and image the C-spine.

questions.text: Case: TBI with hyponatraemia — present it.

steps.bridge: Severity is the post-resuscitation GCS, before sedation. Next: who with this injury needs ICP monitored →
Severe TBI with an abnormal CT gets an ICP monitor. Next: what a falling sodium does to that swollen brain →
Low sodium drives water into astrocytes, so oedema and ICP rise. Next: is the cause SIADH or salt wasting →
Same salty urine, opposite volume: SIADH is euvolaemic, CSW is dry. Next: why restricting fluid is risky in brain injury →
Restriction drops MAP and CPP and worsens CSW, so treat by volume, avoid hypotonic fluid. Next: the emergency 3% bolus →
150 mL of 3% over 20 min, repeated until sodium is up by 5. Next: how far and how fast it may then rise →

spine: Present: young man, fall or RTA, GCS after resuscitation, CT findings, ICP monitor. Day 3–5 sodium falls to 128 with drowsiness or a rising ICP.
Why it matters: hypotonic plasma pulls water into the injured brain, so oedema and ICP rise and CPP falls. Even mild hyponatraemia counts here.
SIADH or CSW: both have low sodium and urine sodium over 30. **Volume status** decides: SIADH euvolaemic, CSW hypovolaemic with high urine output and a negative balance.
What I do: symptoms or raised ICP → **3% saline 150 mL over 20 min**, repeat until sodium is up **5**. Then CSW → isotonic saline, salt, ± fludrocortisone.
SIADH in brain injury: no hypotonic fluids, salt or urea; restrict only if CPP is safe. No vaptan with CNS symptoms.
Caution: rise no more than **10 mmol/L in 24 h** (8 per day after). Fluid restriction in hypovolaemic patients was linked to infarction (Wijdicks 1985).

questions.text: Differentiate SIADH, cerebral salt wasting and diabetes insipidus.

steps.bridge: Urine osmolality over 100 and urine sodium over 30 point to SIAD or salt wasting. Next: how to split those two →
SIAD and CSW share the urine; only volume and urine flow differ. Next: the three-way table with DI added →
SIADH and CSW lose sodium balance, DI loses water; volume decides restrict vs saline. Next: why saline can fail in true SIADH →
Fixed concentrated urine turns isotonic saline into retained free water. Next: the treatment by volume status →

spine: What it is: SIADH and CSW both give low sodium with concentrated, salty urine (Na over 30). DI gives high sodium with dilute urine.
The split: **volume**. SIADH is euvolaemic, normal or low urine flow. CSW is hypovolaemic: high urine output, negative balance, rising haematocrit and urea.
Helpful test: fractional urate excretion stays high (over **11%**) after sodium is corrected in CSW, but normalises in SIADH.
DI: urine over **250 mL/h** for 2 h, urine osmolality under **300**, sodium over 145. Treat with desmopressin 1–2 µg and free water.
What I do: euvolaemic SIADH → fluid restriction, then urea or salt. Hypovolaemic CSW → isotonic saline, salt, fludrocortisone. Severe symptoms in either → 3% saline.
Caution: in SAH and TBI never fluid-restrict; most hyponatraemic SAH patients are volume depleted, and restriction was linked to infarction.

questions.text: How fast do you correct hyponatraemia and what happens if you overcorrect?

steps.bridge: The brain adapts in about 48 h, so fast correction of chronic hyponatraemia shrinks cells: demyelination. Next: the limits →
Rise 5 to relieve oedema; never more than 10 in the first 24 h, 8 after. Next: how the emergency rise is given →
Guidelines give 3% as repeated 150 mL boluses. Next: did a trial test boluses against a slow drip →
SALSA: boluses no more overcorrection than infusion, with less relowering. Next: why overcorrection happens at all →
Restoring volume switches ADH off and a water diuresis overshoots. Next: how desmopressin can clamp that →
Desmopressin clamp: proactive, reactive or rescue, all to stop free-water loss. Next: the exact re-lowering steps →

spine: Why it matters: the brain adapts to chronic hyponatraemia in about 48 h; a fast rise then shrinks cells and causes osmotic demyelination days later.
How fast: aim for **5 mmol/L** in the first hours if symptomatic; limit **10 in 24 h**, then **8** per day (European 2014). US 2013: 10–12, or 8 if high risk.
Evidence: **SALSA** 2021, 178 patients: 3% boluses vs slow infusion, overcorrection **17.2 vs 24.2%** (NS); boluses needed less relowering (41 vs 57%).
Overcorrection: usually a water diuresis once volume, cortisol or drug cause is fixed. Watch urine over 100 mL/h of dilute urine.
Rescue: stop saline, give **10 mL/kg** electrolyte-free water over 1 h and **desmopressin 2 µg IV**, up to 8-hourly. A proactive clamp is 1–2 µg every 6–8 h with 3%.
Caution: newer cohorts show ODS is rare (0.05%) and slow correction carries its own risk; keep the limits strictly for high-risk patients (Na under 105, alcohol, low K).

questions.text: How do you manage hypernatraemia in brain injury?

steps.bridge: Hypernatraemia is too little water for the sodium: loss, pure water loss, or salt gain. Next: the kind we cause on purpose →
Osmotherapy keeps sodium about 145–155 deliberately. Next: how urine osmolality finds the unwanted kind →
Urine osmolality under 300 with high sodium means DI. Next: the formal DI criteria in the ICU →
Polyuria, dilute urine, high serum osmolality; confirm with desmopressin. Next: what changes after brain injury →
Post-TBI DI: 250 mL/h for 2 h, desmopressin 1–2 µg, and the triphasic trap. Next: how to treat central vs nephrogenic DI →
Central DI needs desmopressin and free water; nephrogenic needs thiazide. Next: how much water to give and how fast →

spine: What it is: in brain injury, sodium is either kept high on purpose (osmotherapy, about **145–155**) or rises unwanted from DI or free-water deficit.
Why it matters: hypernatraemia after severe TBI is linked to higher mortality, and early DI often marks severe injury or coming brain death.
Central DI: urine over **250 mL/h for 2 h** without mannitol or diuretic, urine osmolality under **300** (SG under 1.005), sodium over 145 and rising.
What I do: replace losses with free water and give **desmopressin 1–2 µg IV/SC**, repeated when polyuria returns. Check sodium every 6–8 h.
Triphasic response: DI for about a week, then SIADH-like phase for days to 2 weeks, then permanent DI. In phase 2, desmopressin causes hyponatraemia.
Caution: lower chronic hypernatraemia about **0.5 mmol/L/h**, under **10–12 per day**; with raised ICP avoid any fast fall, as rebound oedema can push ICP up.

questions.text: SAH grading scores.

steps.bridge: WFNS uses GCS plus motor deficit; II and III differ only by deficit. Next: the symptom-based scale →
Hunt and Hess grades the clinical picture, 1 to 5. Next: the CT scales that predict vasospasm →
Fisher keys on 1 mm thickness; modified Fisher on thick vs thin plus IVH. Next: the vasospasm risk by grade →
Modified Fisher 0–4: thick cisternal blood with IVH carries the highest risk. Next: when vasospasm comes and who gets it →
Days 4–14; high Fisher grade and female sex predict it. Next: the one drug proven to improve outcome →

spine: What they are: clinical scales grade the patient, CT scales grade the blood. Clinical grade predicts outcome; CT grade predicts vasospasm.
WFNS: GCS plus motor deficit. I = 15; II = 13–14 no deficit; III = 13–14 with deficit; IV = 7–12; V = 3–6. Grades IV–V are poor grade.
Hunt and Hess: 1 mild headache, 2 severe headache or cranial nerve palsy, 3 drowsy or mild focal deficit, 4 stupor or hemiparesis, 5 deep coma.
Modified Fisher (Frontera 2006): 0 none; 1 thin; 2 thin + IVH; 3 thick; 4 thick + IVH. Symptomatic vasospasm about **24, 33, 33, 40%** for grades 1–4.
Other predictors: poor clinical grade and female sex; vasospasm peaks days 4–14, so I monitor with TCD and serial neuro checks.
What I do: **nimodipine 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days** in all patients (Class 1, A); 30 mg 2-hourly if it drops the pressure.

questions.text: Spotter - CT showing subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.bridge: Plain CT is near 100% sensitive in the first days, falling by a week. Next: what to describe on the film →
Describe the blood, its pattern, then IVH and hydrocephalus. Next: the two CT grading scales side by side →
Fisher and modified Fisher share 1–4 but use different criteria. Next: grade this scan on modified Fisher →
