spine: Spot: non-contrast CT with **hyperdense blood** in the basal cisterns (the suprasellar star), sylvian and interhemispheric fissures: subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Pattern: thickest blood hints at the aneurysm: interhemispheric → ACom, sylvian → MCA. Blood only in front of the midbrain may be perimesencephalic, non-aneurysmal.
Complications: look for IVH, hydrocephalus (dilated temporal horns), parenchymal clot and shift.
Grade: modified Fisher 0 none, 1 thin, 2 thin + IVH, 3 thick, 4 thick + IVH. Thick blood with IVH (grade 4) carries the highest vasospasm risk.
Next: CTA for the aneurysm, EVD if hydrocephalus, nimodipine, and secure the aneurysm early. If CT is normal after 6 h but the story fits, LP for xanthochromia.

questions.text: How do you manage vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischaemia after SAH?

steps.bridge: DCI is a new deficit or GCS drop of 2 for over an hour, days 4–14. Next: how TCD picks it up →
Mean MCA velocity over 120 suggests spasm, over 200 severe. Next: how to tell spasm from hyperaemia →
Lindegaard (MCA/ICA) over 3 means spasm; under 3, hyperaemia. Next: the drug every patient gets →
Nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days, the only proven outcome benefit. Next: volume and blood pressure →
Keep euvolaemia; raise BP only for symptomatic DCI, never prophylactically. Next: what became of triple-H →
Triple-H is obsolete: euvolaemia plus induced hypertension replaced it. Next: what to do when spasm is refractory →

spine: What it is: delayed cerebral ischaemia, a new focal deficit or GCS fall of **2 or more** for over an hour, usually **days 4–14**. Angiographic spasm is one cause.
Monitoring: serial neuro exams, TCD (velocity over 120, Lindegaard over 3), CT perfusion or cEEG in poor-grade patients.
Prevention: **nimodipine 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days**; if hypotensive, 30 mg 2-hourly. Keep euvolaemia, sodium normal, avoid fever.
Treatment of DCI: induced hypertension (noradrenaline or phenylephrine) with euvolaemia (AHA/ASA 2023: 2b). Refractory: angioplasty or intra-arterial vasodilators (2b).
Triple-H: no longer used. AHA/ASA 2023 says prophylactic hypervolaemia and haemodynamic augmentation should not be done; they add harm without benefit.
Caution: magnesium, statins and endothelin antagonists do not help. Milrinone is an option, but its load is 0.1–0.2 mg/kg, not 0.5.

questions.text: Acute stroke — thrombolysis and thrombectomy windows.

steps.bridge: Lyse within 4.5 h: alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg. Next: BP around lysis and when to pull the clot →
BP under 185/110 before lysis, 180/105 after; lysis does not bar thrombectomy. Next: how far the windows stretch →

spine: Lysis: disabling ischaemic stroke, CT without bleed, within **4.5 h** of last known well. Wake-up or 4.5–9 h: lyse only if MRI or perfusion imaging shows salvageable brain.
Drugs: **alteplase 0.9 mg/kg** (max 90 mg; 10% bolus, rest over 60 min) or **tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg** (max 25 mg) as one bolus.
Thrombectomy: ICA or M1 occlusion, NIHSS ≥6, within **6 h**, even after lysis. Up to **24 h** with imaging selection; AHA/ASA 2026 adds large cores (ASPECTS **3–5**, age under 80).
Evidence: **DEFUSE-3** (6–16 h, perfusion mismatch) mRS 0–2 45 vs 17%; **DAWN** (6–24 h, clinical–core mismatch) 49 vs 13%.
BP: below **185/110** before lysis and **180/105** for 24 h after. No lysis: treat only above 220/120.
Caution: platelets under 100,000 or a recent bleed exclude lysis. Tenecteplase is non-inferior (AcT 2022) and one bolus suits transfer; 0.4 mg/kg is not recommended.

questions.text: Status epilepticus — management.

steps.bridge: Treat by the clock: benzodiazepine, then a second-line drug, then an anaesthetic infusion. Next: the trial behind the second step →
ESETT: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate are equal, each about half. Next: what to do when they fail →
Refractory SE needs intubation, continuous EEG and an infusion held 24–48 h. Next: the options beyond 24 hours →

spine: What it is: a convulsive seizure beyond **5 min** (ILAE t1), with lasting harm likely after **30 min** (t2). Treat by the clock: ABC, glucose, IV access.
First line at 5 min: lorazepam **0.1 mg/kg** IV (max 4 mg, repeat once) or midazolam **10 mg** IM. Benzodiazepines fail with time as GABA-A receptors are internalised.
Second line at 20 min: levetiracetam **60**, fosphenytoin **20 PE** or valproate **40 mg/kg**. ESETT: equal, about half stopped (**47, 45, 46%**).
Refractory, when a benzodiazepine and one second-line drug fail: intubate, continuous EEG, and a midazolam, propofol or barbiturate infusion.
Titrate to seizure or burst suppression, hold **24–48 h**, then wean. Super-refractory beyond 24 h: ketamine, volatiles, immunotherapy, ketogenic diet.
Caution: find the cause (glucose, sodium, toxins, infection, eclampsia), and suspect non-convulsive status if the patient does not wake.

questions.text: ICU protocol for eclampsia.

steps.bridge: Eclampsia needs three jobs at once: magnesium, BP control and delivery. Next: the magnesium regimen in detail →
Load, maintain to 24 h after delivery, and monitor clinically. Next: the two named regimens and the stop rules →
Pritchard is IM 4-hourly, Zuspan is IV 1 g/h; check reflex, RR and urine before each dose. Next: what toxicity looks like →
Knee jerk goes first, then breathing, then the heart. Next: the drugs that bring BP down →
Labetalol, hydralazine or oral nifedipine, each with its own caution. Next: when to deliver →
Eclampsia means delivery once she is stable, at any gestation. Next: the fluid trap around delivery →
Dry inside despite oedema: restrict fluid, no diuretics. Next: what else causes seizures in pregnancy →

spine: Present: a seizure in pregnancy is eclampsia until proven otherwise. ABC, left lateral, oxygen, prevent injury, then magnesium, BP control and a delivery plan.
Magnesium: Pritchard 4 g IV plus 10 g IM, then 5 g IM 4-hourly; or Zuspan 4 g IV then **1 g/h**. Continue **24 h** after delivery or the last seizure.
BP: treat **≥160/110** that persists 15 min within **30–60 min**, with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or oral nifedipine. Aim for about **140–150/90–100**.
Toxicity signs: knee jerk lost first, then slow breathing, then heart block and arrest. Check reflex, RR ≥16 and urine ≥25–30 mL/h; antidote **calcium gluconate 1 g**.
Deliver once stable: delivery is the definitive treatment. Restrict fluid to about **80 mL/h**, and no diuretics unless there is pulmonary oedema.
Watch for: pulmonary oedema, HELLP, abruption, PRES or bleeding. CT head if focal signs or seizures continue despite magnesium.

questions.text: What is MgSO4 toxicity and how do you monitor it?

steps.bridge: Magnesium blocks calcium and NMDA channels and cuts acetylcholine release. Next: the regimen and target level →
Target 4.8–8.4 mg/dL, monitored at the bedside, not by levels. Next: what each higher level does →
In mg/dL: reflex lost above 9, breathing above 12, arrest above 30. Next: the same ladder in mEq/L and the hourly checks →
Hourly reflex, RR and urine; stop and give calcium if toxic. Next: the exact stop rules and antidote dose →
Withhold if any check fails; calcium gluconate 1 g over about 10 min for respiratory depression. Next: hypermagnesaemia care beyond the antidote →

spine: What it is: magnesium blocks calcium and NMDA channels, cuts acetylcholine release and dilates cerebral vessels. Target **4–7 mEq/L** (4.8–8.4 mg/dL).
Toxicity by level: knee jerk lost at about **7–10 mEq/L**, respiratory depression at **10–13**, conduction block above 15, cardiac arrest above **25**.
Why it builds up: it leaves only through the kidney, so oliguria or renal failure lets it accumulate.
Monitor before each dose and hourly: patellar reflex present, **RR ≥16**, urine **≥25–30 mL/h**, SpO2. Check a level if renal function is poor or reflexes are lost.
What I do: if a check fails, stop or reduce the dose. For respiratory depression, ventilate and give **calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%)** slowly over about 10 min.
Caution: magnesium potentiates neuromuscular blockers. With Pritchard there is no infusion to stop, so I check before every 4-hourly IM dose.

questions.text: What are the ventilation criteria and treatment in Guillain-Barre syndrome?

steps.bridge: GBS climbs legs to arms to breathing to face, with autonomic swings. Next: the numbers that tell you the pump is failing →
VC under 20, MIP weaker than −30, MEP under 40, or a 30% fall. Next: who will need it, predicted on admission →
EGRIS 5–7 means about 65% ventilated in week 1. Next: the bedside triggers and the drug to avoid at intubation →
Intubate on the trend and bulbar weakness, never with suxamethonium. Next: the two treatments that shorten the disease →
IVIG and plasma exchange are equal; never both in sequence, no steroids. Next: the autonomic traps while you wait →

spine: What it is: acute immune polyneuropathy, ascending and areflexic; **20–30%** need ventilation, and SpO₂ and gases fall late.
Ventilation criteria, the 20/30/40 rule: VC **<20 mL/kg**, MIP weaker than **−30**, MEP **<40 cmH₂O**, or a **>30%** fall.
Predict on admission with EGRIS (**0–7**): fast onset, facial or bulbar weakness, low MRC. **5–7 = 65%** ventilated in week 1; EAN/PNS 2023 prefers modified EGRIS.
What I do: elective intubation on the trend, bulbar weakness or fatigue; no suxamethonium; watch bradycardia on suction.
Treatment: **IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5** within 2 weeks, or **plasma exchange 4–5 sessions (12–15 L)** within 4 weeks: equal.
Caution: no steroids, no exchange followed by IVIG, no routine second IVIG course (EAN/PNS 2023).

questions.text: How do you manage myasthenic crisis?

steps.bridge: Crisis is weakness needing ventilation, usually set off by infection. Next: the drugs that can tip a myasthenic over →
Aminoglycosides, quinolones, macrolides, magnesium and β-blockers worsen it. Next: the numbers that say intubate →
VC under 15, NIF weaker than −20, PEmax under 40: not the GBS rule. Next: how to intubate and ventilate safely →
RSI, low-dose non-depolariser, stop pyridostigmine while ventilated. Next: the treatment that ends the crisis →
Plasma exchange or IVIG, equal in trials, exchange a little faster. Both wear off. Next: what bridges beyond 3 weeks →
Steroids follow, under ventilatory cover, as they can worsen weakness first. Next: is it myasthenic or cholinergic? →

spine: What it is: myasthenic weakness needing ventilation or airway protection; **15–20%** of patients, mostly after infection or a drug.
Monitor: intubate at VC **<15 mL/kg**, NIF weaker than **−20** or PEmax **<40 cmH₂O**; bulbar weakness may force it earlier.
What I do: RSI with a low-dose non-depolariser, stop pyridostigmine while ventilated, treat the trigger, stop offending drugs.
Treatment: **plasma exchange (5 sessions)** or **IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5**; equal in trials, exchange faster by consensus; steroids alongside.
Myasthenic vs cholinergic: cholinergic is too much pyridostigmine: small pupils, secretions, bradycardia, fasciculations.
Caution: edrophonium is largely abandoned (off the US market since 2018); if unsure, secure the airway and stop the anticholinesterase, which settles both.

questions.text: How do you manage tetanus in the ICU?

steps.bridge: The toxin removes spinal inhibition; Ablett IV adds autonomic storm. Next: how to stop more toxin reaching the nerves →
Debride, one IM antitoxin dose, metronidazole, then vaccinate. Next: does putting antitoxin in the CSF do better? →
Intrathecal is safe but unproven where ventilation exists (Van Hao 2022). Next: controlling spasms and the autonomic storm →
Magnesium spares sedatives, relaxants and verapamil but not ventilation. Next: how to spot magnesium toxicity →

spine: What it is: tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory interneurons: rigidity, spasms, autonomic storm. Ablett I–IV; grade IV = autonomic instability.
Stop the toxin: debride the wound, one IM dose of human antitoxin (CDC **500 IU**), metronidazole or penicillin, then toxoid.
Spasms: benzodiazepines in a quiet room, early airway, relaxants and ventilation, often about **16 days**, so plan a tracheostomy.
Magnesium (Thwaites, Lancet 2006, n = **195**): no fall in ventilation (OR **0.71**, NS), but less midazolam, pipecuronium and verapamil.
Route: intrathecal looked good in old trials (Kabura 2006, RR **0.71**), but Van Hao 2022: ventilation **43% vs 50%**, NS. I give IM.
Caution: titrate magnesium to a present knee jerk (serum **2–4 mmol/L**); recovery gives no immunity, so complete vaccination.

questions.text: What are the ICU targets in acute spinal cord injury?

steps.bridge: ASIA grade, MAP support, no hypotonic fluid, VTE prophylaxis within 72 h. Next: where the steroid story started →
NASCIS II and III suggested an early steroid benefit that did not hold up. Next: the 2024 MAP update, early surgery and today's steroid positions →

spine: What I target: no hypotension or hypoxia. MAP floor **75–80 mmHg**, no active push above **90–95**, for about **3–7 days** (AO Spine/Praxis 2024, updating AANS/CNS 2013).
Why: the injured cord loses autoregulation, and neurogenic shock is common, so hypoperfusion adds secondary ischaemia. The old target was **85–90 for 7 days**, from Level III data.
Evidence: a 2025 RCT (92 patients) of MAP >85–90 vs >65–70 found no neurological gain but more respiratory complications (**78% vs 39%**).
Also: decompression **within 24 h** (strong, 2024), VTE prophylaxis **within 72 h**, no hypotonic fluids, close watch on breathing and heart rate in cervical injury.
Steroids: NASCIS II gave methylprednisolone **30 mg/kg then 5.4 mg/kg/h for 23 h**; the primary outcome was negative and the <8 h benefit was post hoc.
Now: AANS/CNS 2013 says **not recommended**. AO Spine 2017 (weak) suggests offering a 24-h course only if started **within 8 h**, not a 48-h course. I do not give it routinely.

questions.text: How do you declare brain stem death in India?

steps.bridge: THOA 1994 made brainstem death legal death in India; THOTA rules followed in 2014. Next: what must be true before you test →
Known cause, no drugs or paralysis, temp >36, SBP >100, metabolic causes corrected. Next: the reflexes that must all be absent →
Pupils, corneal, gag, cough, oculocephalic and caloric all absent; spinal reflexes allowed. Next: how to run the apnoea test →
Pre-oxygenate, disconnect, O2 at the carina, ABG at 8–10 min, PaCO2 ≥60 and ≥20 rise. Next: what to do when you cannot complete it →
Ancillary tests only when the exam or apnoea test cannot be completed. Next: who certifies under Indian law →
A board of four, two examinations at least 6 h apart. Next: the 2026 national guideline numbers and the live court question →

spine: Law: **THOA 1994** (Rules 2014) recognises brain stem death. A board of four certifies on **Form 10**: medical administrator, authorised specialist, neurologist or neurosurgeon, treating doctor.
Prerequisites: known irreversible cause, no sedatives or paralysis, temp **≥36 °C**, SBP **≥100** (MAP ≥60), metabolic and endocrine causes corrected (2026 national guideline).
Exam: deep coma; pupils, corneal, oculocephalic, cold caloric, gag and cough all absent. Spinal reflexes are allowed.
Apnoea test: 100% O₂ for **10 min**, disconnect, O₂ catheter at the carina **4–6 L/min**, watch **8–10 min**, ABG. Positive: no breath with PaCO₂ **≥60 and ≥20 above baseline**.
Twice: two examinations at least **6 h apart** in adults. Abort if SBP **<90** or SpO₂ **<85% for >30 s**, then an ancillary test.
Caution: in Apr 2026 the Supreme Court asked AIIMS for an expert review of apnoea test safety and its alternatives; judgment reserved. So I follow Form 10 exactly, independent of donation.
